title: IPL Auction Game
oneLiner: A live cricket auction game: bid on 323 players with friends, or solo against 9 AI franchises driven by trained reinforcement learning bots.
description: A full IPL mega auction you can play in the browser. Bid live against your friends on 323 players while the server keeps every purse, squad and timer in sync over Socket.IO and Redis. Play solo and you face 9 AI franchises, each with its own bidding personality (Moneyball, Star Chaser, Balanced Builder or Opportunist), and the auction ends with awards and team rankings.
built: A React front end and an Express and Socket.IO server for live bidding
Purse management, player stats, auction awards and rankings
Bot opponents, with A2C and OpenAI-ES experiments recorded in the repo
My own deployment scripts for Ubuntu and systemd
broke: MongoDB 8 needed a compatibility workaround on the Ubuntu 24.04 kernel.
Wrong permissions on a temporary staging directory caused 403 errors after deploys.
why: My friends and I used to run IPL auctions by hand: writing out player lists, calling players one by one, running the bidding and tracking everyone's budget. It was fun, but a hassle. I also wanted to build something people could actually play, not another CRUD app. So I built a site that runs the whole auction, and it grew into a full IPL mega auction with realistic bidding, team strategy and multiplayer. And yes, I genuinely love cricket.
learned: A real-time multiplayer app is much harder than it looks. I learned Socket.IO and Redis, room management, keeping state in sync between players, handling disconnects and reconnects, and auction logic that behaves the same for everyone. Most of all, I learned how to turn a simple real-world idea into a full product.

title: RepoMind AI
oneLiner: Builds a temporal knowledge graph of a Git repository to detect architecture drift and reconstruct the decisions behind the code.
description: Point it at a Git repository and it builds a knowledge graph of the code in Neo4j: which modules depend on which, and how that changed commit by commit. It checks the architecture rules against the real dependency graph, gives the repo a health score, and finds the exact commit where a layer first got skipped. It also reconstructs the decisions behind the code, writes docs, and answers questions in a chat that shows the queries it ran.
built: Architecture rules checked against the real dependency graph, with a health score
Drift over time, rebuilding the architecture at any point in a repo's history
Reconstructed decision records, generated docs and an ask-the-repo chat that shows its queries
An evaluation suite: 150 of 150 seeded violations detected across Python, JavaScript and TypeScript fixtures
why: Understanding a large codebase that someone else built is hard. As a repository grows, its architecture, the reasons behind its decisions and the way its parts depend on each other all get harder to see. I wanted to find out whether an AI system could go beyond answering questions about the code and actually rebuild the architectural understanding of a project.
learned: An agentic AI system is very different from connecting an LLM to a few tools. You have to think about how agents communicate, how information is retrieved and kept, how decisions are checked, and how the whole workflow copes with wrong outputs. It made me appreciate how much architecture matters in AI applications.

title: Mimic Hunt
oneLiner: A 3D multiplayer prop hunt in the browser, where hiders disguise themselves as furniture in a low-poly mansion.
description: A prop hunt for 2 to 10 friends, played in the browser. Hiders disguise themselves as one of 35 pieces of furniture in a 3D mansion with 11 connected areas, and Hunters have to work out which chair or lamp is really a player. The server runs the game and checks every move and shot, so a Hunter never learns where a hider is unless they can see them. It works on phones too, with a joystick and swipe-to-look.
built: Private rooms for 2 to 10 players, joined with a code or invite link
A 60 × 72 m mansion with 11 connected areas, about 320 objects and 35 disguises
A server-authoritative game, where a Hunter's client never receives hiders it cannot see
Touch controls for phones: joystick, swipe-to-look and drag-to-aim
broke: In the first playtests one side won almost every round. I fixed it with game design, not just code: radar sweeps that show only which room a hider is in, decoys that hiders can leave behind, bigger penalties for Hunters who shoot random furniture, and a smaller map.
A reconnect loop leak, a damage stat cap and mismatched models and hitboxes all needed fixing.
The game gave no readable error when the server was unreachable, until I added one.
why: I wanted a real multiplayer game that my friends and I could play together, not a single-player demo. We play it over the same Wi-Fi, on laptops and phones.
learned: Making a multiplayer game work is only half the job. Making it fair is the other half. Fair for both teams meant watching people play and asking why the game stopped being fun for one side. Fair against cheating meant making the server the single source of truth: it checks every move, shot and disguise, and never tells a Hunter's browser where a hider is unless that Hunter can see them.

title: Clipper
oneLiner: A local AI video clipper that finds and scores short moments in long videos, with no paid API and no cloud.
description: Give it a long video and it finds the moments worth turning into Shorts or Reels. It transcribes the speech with faster-whisper, analyses the audio and scene changes, asks a local model through Ollama to judge each candidate, and gives every moment a score from 0 to 100. You review the clips in the browser, approve or edit them, and export them with FFmpeg, all on your own machine with no paid API and no cloud.
built: A full pipeline: transcribe, analyse audio and scenes, find moments, score, select, review, export
A 0 to 100 score that combines model judgements with deterministic length and audio checks
A browser review screen to preview, approve, reject and edit clips
166 passing tests, as recorded in the development log
broke: My first real video, a 20-minute Hindi and English interview, came back as garbled transcript. Average word confidence was 58%.
Transcription took 51 minutes on CPU because a GPU DLL was missing. After the fix it took 3.6 minutes.
Normal speech sat above the excitement threshold, so talking counted as a highlight: 74 false events, then 0 after the fix.
why: Short videos are everywhere, but cutting them from long ones means watching hours of footage, finding the good moments and editing every clip. With Shorts and Reels so popular, I wanted to see how much of that AI could take over.
learned: An AI product is much more than the model. The real work is the reliable system around it: FFmpeg and FFprobe, transcription, highlight detection, GPU and CPU tuning, different video formats, word-highlighted captions, and pipelines that resume and cache their work. Good AI output depends as much on the input and the engineering around it as on the model.

title: SolveFX
oneLiner: A Chrome extension that turns LeetCode verdicts into cinematic moments, with a different sound and overlay for each result.
description: A Chrome extension that watches your LeetCode submissions and reacts to the verdict. Accepted gets a celebration, Wrong Answer gets “So close. Probably.”, Time Limit Exceeded fakes a system shutdown, and runtime, memory and compile errors each get their own screen and sound. It runs inside LeetCode's own page, so solving problems works exactly as before.
built: Verdict detection on LeetCode submissions
A different overlay and sound for accepted, wrong answer, time limit, runtime, memory and compile results
why: Solving LeetCode problems is hard enough, so I wanted to make it a little more fun, and make an Accepted feel more satisfying. It was also a chance to try browser extensions and to work inside a website someone else built.
learned: Chrome extension development, JavaScript, and DOM work inside an existing site instead of building everything from scratch. It also taught me that even small ideas become interesting projects when you pay attention to the user experience.

title: Image Captions on AWS
oneLiner: Upload a photo and get a caption, through a serverless pipeline on AWS.
description: Upload a photo and a serverless pipeline writes a caption for it. The image is stored in Amazon S3, and a Lambda function asks Amazon Rekognition what is in it, then hands those labels to a model on Amazon Bedrock to write a natural sentence. The caption is saved to DynamoDB, and a small Python front end handles uploads.
built: A Lambda function that reads labels from Rekognition and asks a Bedrock model for a caption
Image storage in S3 and captions saved to DynamoDB
A small Python front end for uploads

title: CareerPilot
oneLiner: An agentic job-search platform with a transparent matching engine, and it never submits an application without your approval.
description: An agentic job-search platform. It finds jobs, scores each one against your profile with a deterministic matching engine that shows why, and tracks every application through an explicit state machine. Its one hard rule: it never submits an application without your approval of the exact form. Built with FastAPI, PostgreSQL with pgvector, and React.
built: Job discovery and deterministic scoring against your profile
Application tracking through an explicit state machine

title: Daylyt
oneLiner: An installable, offline-first tracker for workouts, food, sleep, habits and focus.
description: A private tracker for your whole day: workouts, food, water, sleep, steps, habits, tasks and focus, with a weekly planner, streaks and statistics. It has about 990 exercises and 7,600 foods built in, including Indian dishes you can log in katoris and bowls. It installs like an app, works offline, and syncs to Firestore, so a new phone never loses your data.
built: Tracking for workouts, food, water, sleep, steps, habits, tasks and focus
A weekly planner, streaks and statistics, with sync so data survives a new phone

title: Digital Twin RL
oneLiner: A research platform that pairs a discrete-event simulation of a shop floor with reinforcement learning for scheduling and energy optimisation.
description: A research platform for smart manufacturing. A SimPy simulation of a shop floor, with machines, job arrivals, breakdowns and energy use, is wrapped as a Gymnasium environment so reinforcement learning agents can learn to schedule the jobs. It benchmarks six RL algorithms against classic dispatching rules under identical conditions, on both production efficiency and energy.
built: A discrete-event digital twin of a manufacturing shop floor
A Gymnasium-compatible environment for training scheduling agents
